title: Playwright Fundamentals — Selectors and Waits
subtitle: Auto-waits exist. Stop sleeping. Stop using CSS selectors built from BEM hell.

audioChapters.label: Opening — why Selenium veterans get Playwright wrong
Mental model: Playwright auto-waits, stop sleeping

blocks.notesByline: Notes by Sneha, SDET batch of 2024

blocks.md:
Selenium veterans show up to Playwright and immediately write the same test they wrote in 2018: `await driver.findElement(By.css('.btn.btn-primary.checkout-btn-v2'))` followed by `await driver.sleep(3000)` followed by an assertion that lies because the page hadn't finished hydrating. Playwright doesn't need any of that, but the muscle memory is hard to break.

This lesson is about the two things Playwright does differently and the two named moves that make your tests resilient. By the end you'll write tests that survive a designer renaming half your CSS classes.

blocks.title: Mental model: Playwright auto-waits, stop sleeping
blocks.md:
Every Playwright action — `click`, `fill`, `selectOption`, `expect(...).toBeVisible()` — does **actionability checks** before it runs. It waits for the element to be attached, visible, stable, enabled, and on top. It retries assertions until they pass or the timeout (default 5 seconds) hits.

This means: **you almost never need `waitForTimeout`**. If your test sleeps, your test is wrong. The only legitimate uses for arbitrary sleep are (1) you genuinely cannot detect when a long-running animation has stopped, and (2) you're debugging. Both should be temporary. Anything else is a flake-factory you'll regret in 3 months.

blocks.caption: Watch a Playwright `click` walk through the actionability checks: attached → visible → stable → enabled → on top → fire.

hi-IN.title: Intern ne 47 sleep daal diye
hi-IN.md: Intern ko CI green chahiye tha demo ke liye. Pehla sleep — `await page.waitForTimeout(1000)`. Phir 2000. Phir 3000. End mein 47 sleeps. Build green ho gaya. Demo ho gaya. Prod red ho gaya kyunki actual race condition tha. Senior dev ne intern ko bola: "beta, sleep tumhare problem ko hide karta hai, fix nahi karta. Aur on-call mujhe page karega 3am ko, tujhe nahi."
hi-IN.attribution: — overheard at a Bengaluru WeWork pantry

en.title: Intern added 47 sleeps
en.md: An intern needed CI green for a demo. First sleep: `await page.waitForTimeout(1000)`. Then 2000. Then 3000. By the end, 47 sleep statements. Build went green. Demo happened. Prod went red, because the underlying race condition was still there. Senior dev to intern: 'sleep hides your problem, it doesn't fix it. And on-call gets paged at 3am, not you.'

blocks.md:
**CSS selectors are the problem, not the solution.** When you write `page.locator('.btn.btn-primary.checkout-v2')`, you're coupling your test to your designer's mood. Half your test failures will come from style refactors that did not change a single user-visible thing.

Playwright's role-based locators are the opposite: they identify elements the way a screen reader (and a human) does. `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay ₹1,200' })` finds the button labelled "Pay ₹1,200" regardless of class names, regardless of whether it's a `<button>` or a `<div role='button'>`, regardless of which framework re-rendered it last.

The locator priority you should burn into your fingertips:

1. `getByRole` — for anything interactive. The default.
2. `getByLabel` — for form fields with visible labels.
3. `getByText` — for static content you're verifying.
4. `getByTestId` — for elements with no useful semantics, where the team agrees on a `data-testid`.
5. CSS / XPath — only when the above genuinely don't work. With a comment explaining why.

**The named move:** *getByRole over CSS*. If you're reaching for `.locator('.foo')` your first instinct should be: "is there a role here I'm ignoring?"

blocks.title: Translation: from a customer journey to a Playwright locator

steps.label: 1. The customer journey, in English
steps.body: A user lands on the pricing page, clicks 'Start free trial', fills email and password, agrees to terms, and clicks 'Create account'.

steps.label: 2. Find the role for each interaction
steps.body: Click → button. Fill → textbox (with label). Toggle → checkbox. Final click → button.

steps.label: 3. Use the visible name as the locator key
steps.body: What does the human see on the button? 'Start free trial', 'Create account'. That's your name.

steps.label: 4. The test now reads like the journey
steps.body: If a non-engineer reads it aloud, they understand it. That's the test for whether your locators are right.

steps.label: 5. Designer renames `.btn-primary-v3` to `.btn-cta-2026`. Test still passes.
steps.body: Because the test never knew or cared about the class name. That's the whole point.

blocks.prompt: Which Playwright locator should you reach for *first* when targeting a 'Submit order' button?

choices.label: page.locator('.btn.btn-primary.submit-order-v2')
choices.explain: CSS-class chains are the most fragile selectors and the most common cause of refactor-induced flake. Skip.

choices.label: page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit order' })
choices.explain: Role-based, name-based, framework-agnostic. This is the default. Use it.

choices.label: page.getByTestId('submit-order-btn')
choices.explain: Test IDs are fine as a last resort, but reaching for them first means you skip the more semantic options. Burn the role first.

choices.label: page.locator('xpath=//button[contains(text(), "Submit")]')
choices.explain: XPath in 2026 is a code smell. There's almost always a better Playwright API. Use it only when nothing else works and leave a comment.

hi-IN.title: Designer ne sab CSS rename kar diya
hi-IN.md: Designer ne Friday shaam ko design system migrate kiya. `.btn-primary` ban gaya `.button-action-primary`. Soomvar ko 412 tests red. Dev team ne saturday-sunday spend kiya CSS find-replace mein. QA team ne `getByRole` waale 38 tests run kiye — sab green. QA ne pizza party demand ki aur jeet gayi.
hi-IN.attribution: — a peaceful weekend, not enjoyed by the dev team

en.title: Designer renamed all the CSS
en.md: Designer migrated the design system on Friday evening. `.btn-primary` became `.button-action-primary`. Monday morning: 412 tests red. Dev team spent the weekend on find-replace. QA team ran their 38 `getByRole` tests — all green. QA demanded a pizza party and won.

coach.name: Test-Sensei Tarun
coach.role: Principal SDET, today reviewing a PR titled 'fix: add 12 sleeps'

intro: You're code-reviewing 6 Playwright snippets. Tarun is loitering with opinions.
Mark each as 'ship it', 'needs work', or 'reject and rewrite'.

scenarios.explain: Role-based, named, no sleep, no CSS. Textbook.
The 2-second sleep is doing nothing the auto-retry wouldn't do. Delete the timeout.
Lost the retry by awaiting first. Rewrite as `await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toHaveText('Hello');`.
Coupled to CSS classes. One refactor away from breaking. Use `getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' })`.
Bumped timeout for a known-slow operation. Reasonable. Comment why if not obvious.
Test IDs with dynamic IDs in them are fragile. Better: `page.getByRole('row', { name: /Order 12345/ })`.

blocks.title: The classic trap: awaiting the value before asserting it

blocks.prompt: Order these locator strategies from most preferred (top) to last resort (bottom):
blocks.hint: The order matches Playwright's official guidance: semantics first, structural CSS last.

blocks.instruction: Rewrite this Selenium-flavoured Playwright test to use role-based locators and web-first assertions. Remove all sleeps. Assume the form has visible labels.

blocks.prompt: Which of these are signs of well-written Playwright tests? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: Locators read like the user journey: 'click the Pay button, fill the email field, ...'
choices.explain: Yes. Semantic locators describe behaviour, not structure. They survive refactors.

choices.label: Most assertions are `await expect(locator).to...()` with no intermediate variable extraction
choices.explain: Yes. Web-first assertions retry; extracting to a variable first defeats the retry.

choices.label: Strategic `waitForTimeout` calls placed after every navigation 'just to be safe'
choices.explain: These are flake bombs in waiting. Playwright's auto-wait already handles navigation. Sleeps hide problems they don't solve.

choices.label: CSS class selectors only appear in one shared `selectors.ts` file with comments explaining why each is needed
choices.explain: Centralising bad selectors doesn't make them good. The right answer is to not need them in the first place.

hi-IN.title: Mere laptop pe pass hota hai
hi-IN.md: Dev: "mere laptop pe pass hota hai." QA: "CI pe fail hota hai." Dev: "sleep 5000 daal do." QA: "sleep daalne se kya hoga, race condition theek nahi hota." Dev: "toh main local pe sleep daal ke check karta hoon." QA ne dev ko keyboard se mara. Sahi kiya.

en.title: It works on my laptop
en.md: Dev: "works on my laptop." QA: "fails in CI." Dev: "add a sleep 5000." QA: "sleep doesn't fix the race condition." Dev: "let me add a sleep locally to check." QA hit dev with the keyboard. Justified.

points: Playwright auto-waits for elements to be actionable. If your test sleeps, your test is wrong.
Reach for getByRole first. CSS selectors are the problem, not the solution.
Web-first assertions (`expect(locator).to...()`) auto-retry. If you extract the value to a variable first, you've broken the retry loop.
The locator priority ladder: role → label → text → test ID → CSS, in that order. The bottom rungs should sting to use.
Tests that read like the user journey survive design refactors. Tests coupled to class names die in them.

blocks.prompt: Open one of your existing Playwright (or Selenium / Cypress) tests right now. How many CSS selectors does it use? How many sleeps? How many assertions extract a value before checking it? Pick one of those three and rewrite a single test to remove them. Notice how much shorter the file gets.
